\chapter{Good Night}
\label{ch:hi-good-night}
\hlchaptermodality{27}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can wish someone good night in Hindi and say why the phrase uses literary \hi{रात्रि} rather than everyday \hi{रात}.}

Say \hi{शुभ} \hi{रात्रि} at parting, name the raat / rātri register pair, and trace śubh from 'to shine' to 'auspicious'.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[śubh rātri]{\hi{शुभ} \hi{रात्रि} (śubh rātri) — \textquotedblleft{}good night,\textquotedblright{} the formal doublet in action}

\label{lesson:HI-C27-shubh-raatri}



\begin{quote}
Hindi keeps two versions of \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{} side by side — one for everyday speech, one for set phrases. Here's where the formal one gets used.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{शुभ} \hi{रात्रि} — \textquotedblleft{}auspicious night\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{\hi{शुभ} \hi{रात्रि}} (\textbf{śubh rātri}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{good night}\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{auspicious night}.\textquotedblright{} Notice: this uses \textbf{\hi{रात्रि}} (\emph{rātri}), the very Sanskrit word last lesson's \emph{raat} descended \textbf{from} — but here, kept in its \textbf{full, unworn Sanskrit} form. This is a classic \textbf{tatsama/tadbhava doublet}: \emph{rātri} (\textbf{tatsama}, a direct, unchanged Sanskrit borrowing) sits alongside \emph{raat} (\textbf{tadbhava}, the same word worn down by centuries of ordinary sound change) — Hindi keeps both, one for everyday speech, one for set formal phrases like this one.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{शुभ} — \textquotedblleft{}auspicious,\textquotedblright{} from a root meaning \textquotedblleft{}to shine\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{\hi{शुभ}} (\textbf{śubh}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{auspicious, good, fortunate}\textquotedblright{} — comes from the Sanskrit verbal root \textbf{\hi{शुभ्}} (\emph{śubh}), whose core sense is \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to be beautiful, splendid}.\textquotedblright{} This traces to a well-sourced \textbf{Proto-Indo-European} root, \emph{\textbf{*\'{k}ewb\textsuperscript{h}-}} (\textquotedblleft{}to be beautiful\textquotedblright{}). Some scholars propose a \textbf{further, more speculative} connection beyond that — to \emph{*(s)kewh\textsubscript{1}-} (\textquotedblleft{}to perceive\textquotedblright{}) or \emph{*\'{k}ew-} (\textquotedblleft{}to shine\textquotedblright{}) — but that deeper link, not the \emph{*\'{k}ewb\textsuperscript{h}-} root itself, is the genuinely uncertain part. Either way, the underlying idea is a familiar one: \textbf{auspiciousness imagined as a kind of radiance or beauty} — something good \textquotedblleft{}shines.\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}śubh rātri\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}good night,\textquotedblright{} literally \textquotedblleft{}auspicious night\textquotedblright{}
  \item the formal doublet — rātri here, raat in everyday speech
  \item śubh's own root — śubh, \textquotedblleft{}to shine\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}auspicious\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does \textbf{\hi{शुभ} \hi{रात्रि}} use the everyday \emph{raat} or the formal \emph{rātri}? (\textbf{The formal \emph{rātri}} — Hindi keeps both versions, one for everyday speech, one for set phrases.) What does \textbf{\hi{शुभ}} literally trace back to? (A root meaning \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to be beautiful, splendid},\textquotedblright{} PIE \emph{*\'{k}ewb\textsuperscript{h}-} — auspiciousness as a kind of radiance.) Is that root itself uncertain, or is a \emph{further} proposed connection the shakier part? (\textbf{The root \emph{*\'{k}ewb\textsuperscript{h}-} itself is well-sourced} — it's the \emph{deeper} proposed link, to \textquotedblleft{}to shine\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}to perceive,\textquotedblright{} that's genuinely speculative.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṭa]{\hi{ट} — one run, then the headline}

\label{lesson:HI-S142-letter-ta-retroflex}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \textbf{\hi{फ}} — how many pen lifts did it take?

This one takes fewer.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{ट}}
\textbf{\hi{ट}} — \emph{ṭa}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a descending central stem joined to a counterclockwise \textbf{open} round body
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

The word \emph{open} is doing real work there. The round part comes back up toward the stem and \textbf{stops short of meeting it}, leaving a gap at the upper right. Keep that gap when you draw it.

\subsection*{Script: the tongue goes back}
\textbf{\hi{ट}} is a \textbf{retroflex}: the tongue curls back and taps the roof of the mouth, further back than it goes for \textbf{\hi{त}}. Two different letters for what an English ear hears as one \emph{t}, and Hindi uses both.

Words that were yours long before this page:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{रोटी}} — bread
  \item \textbf{\hi{घंटा}} — an hour
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{ट}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the central stem's headline junction, descend, turn left through the upper shoulder, and sweep counterclockwise around the open round body to its up-right tip without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 1.} Everything below the headline is one unbroken run, and only \textbf{\hi{ढ}} is built the same way.

\begin{quote}
Verified two-stroke teaching form fitted to the bundled printed outline; everyday handwriting may narrow or simplify the curve differently.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\hi{ट}-order.gif’, strokes 1–2, Wikimedia Commons, 10 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two words and find \hi{ट} in each one
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{रोटी}  ·  \hi{घंटा}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{ट} three times, saying \emph{ṭa} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Say it:} where the gap in this letter is
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many pen lifts does \textbf{\hi{ट}} take? (One.) Where does the tongue go for it, compared with \textbf{\hi{त}}? (Further back.) Name a food you have asked for that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
